entries.test: Public records of GPT-5 development and capabilities as of publication, together with Marcus's predictions from a year earlier, would establish whether these outcomes and delays matched his prediction.
entries.note: The claim concerns the situation at publication, not subsequent GPT-5 capabilities.

entries.test: GPT-4.5's released capabilities and independent evaluations would establish whether it solved hallucination and reasoning problems as the preceding paragraph describes the expectations for GPT-5.
entries.note: The preceding paragraph supplies concrete content for the expectations comparison.
“Unlikely” expresses a probability rather than a firm outcome.
Marcus endorses this assessment in his own voice while citing The Information; “unlikely” remains probabilistic.

entries.test: Published evaluations of scaled deep learning systems available at publication would establish whether reasoning errors and hallucinations persisted.
entries.note: This asserts persistence of problems, not absence of improvement.
“Looks to be true” gives a tentative assessment of the forthcoming model.
“Setting the world on fire” could concern reception, adoption, or capabilities. The normalization selects technical advances without sufficient support.

entries.test: Public comparisons of capability gains against increases in training compute, data, and model size across successive generations would establish whether returns to scaling had diminished by publication.
entries.note: The plain contextual reading is diminishing capability gains from scaling.

entries.test: Public scaling and capability results across major AI developers would establish whether diminishing returns were widespread rather than confined to OpenAI at publication.
entries.note: “The whole field” refers contextually to the industry-wide scaling trend.

entries.test: Public economic studies estimating generative AI's contribution to GDP through publication would establish whether its aggregate impact was very small.
entries.note: The claim concerns realized aggregate impact, not projected future benefits.
This recommends how investors should assess Nvidia.
The principal claim is investment advice; the description of Nvidia's pitch is a separable factual assertion.

entries.test: Public industry revenue estimates before the price wars and cumulative generative AI expenditure estimates through publication would establish whether the stated orders of magnitude were accurate.
entries.note: The normalization omits the material “pre price wars” qualification on revenue. Its numerical core is checkable, although the recommendation to compare figures is normative.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures and industry estimates of generative AI revenue and costs at publication would establish whether the industry was operating profitably.
entries.note: The surrounding revenue and expenditure comparison supplies a plain financial reading.

entries.test: Public economic research estimating generative AI's realized contribution to aggregate productivity through publication would establish whether that contribution was minimal.
entries.note: The GDP discussion supports an aggregate reading rather than a claim about every individual task.
“Prospects ... aren’t looking great” specifies neither an outcome nor a shared standard for assessing those prospects.

entries.test: Public model evaluations at publication would establish whether the reasoning and hallucination problems identified in the post remained unresolved.
entries.note: Earlier discussion gives “basic problems” concrete referents.
The post supplies no shared criterion distinguishing “minor variations” from substantial advances across releases.
